post_text:
I assumed Cassandra's default write paths would handle our massive audit spikes without explicitly tuning quorum settings.

The schema migration ran silently, finishing in record time with zero errors reported on the monitoring dashboard.

As a JVM engineer refactoring a fragile compliance pipeline, I swapped our strained relational tables for a distributed Cassandra ring.

The deployment succeeded instantly, dropping write latencies to sub-millisecond levels and making the new architecture look like an immediate triumph.

A hollow feeling set in an hour later when downstream reconciliation jobs began failing. We were executing both writes and reads at `LOCAL_ONE`, allowing queries to hit uncoordinated nodes before data ever replicated across the cluster.

The database wasn't actually fast; it was merely serving stale ghost records and masking severe data loss behind glowing green metrics.

What I learned:

Speed achieved by relaxing database consistency is never an architectural victory; it is an unbacked loan paid back in silent corruption.
